extracted.intended_audience: public health communicators and media/press officers (federal, state, local) who draft crisis press releases and public messaging
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting press releases and other public messages during public-health emergencies (crisis & emergency risk communication — CERC). Focuses on what to say, how to say it, timing, tone, audience tailoring, and coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be First
rubrics_metrics.description: Get accurate information out quickly — provide initial information as soon as possible rather than remaining silent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release timely initial statements even if all details are not available. State what you know, what you don’t yet know, and when more information will be available. Anti-pattern: prolonged silence that allows rumors to fill the gap. Example: publish initial press release within hours with basic facts and planned next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Right
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide accurate, evidence-based information; verify facts before releasing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check data, sources, and numbers for accuracy. If numbers change, explain why. Use plain explanations for technical details. Scoring note: accuracy and clarity of facts are primary quality measures. Anti-pattern: releasing speculative figures or technical jargon without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Build and maintain trust through honesty, transparency, and consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge uncertainties, correct mistakes promptly, cite credible sources, and avoid over-reassurance. Consistent messaging across spokespeople and partners increases credibility. Example: if guidance changes, explain the new evidence and why recommendations are updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express Empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge and validate the public’s fears, concerns, and hardships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language that recognizes real impacts (loss, inconvenience, fear) and avoids minimizing. Opening sentences that show concern improve reception. Anti-pattern: purely technical or detached messaging that ignores human impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear, specific, and feasible actions the audience can take to reduce risk or get help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State concrete steps (what to do, how to do it, where to get help) and explain why the actions matter. Prioritize 1–3 key actions in every release (call to action). Use checklists or bullet points for clarity. Anti-pattern: describing risk without giving actionable guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate respectfully to diverse populations and avoid blaming or stigmatizing language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use culturally sensitive phrasing, appropriate translations, and accessibility formats. Avoid language that singles out or blames groups. Tailor tone and examples to the audience’s context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Plain Language and Clear Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in simple, non‑technical language; structure releases so the most important information comes first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short sentences, active voice, and common words. Lead with the key message (lead paragraph) and follow with supporting details. Include headings, bullets, and FAQs where appropriate. Anti-pattern: long paragraphs of technical prose or unexplained acronyms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the Primary Message
rubrics_metrics.description: Make one clear primary message and repeat it; all parts of the release should support that message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the single most important point for this audience (e.g., a protective action or new risk). Put it in the headline and first paragraph; repeat it later. Avoid burying the primary message in secondary details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Transparent About What Is Unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: State uncertainties plainly and explain what is being done to learn more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data are incomplete, say so and describe ongoing investigations or next reporting times. This reduces speculation and preserves trust. Anti-pattern: pretending certainty or withholding information that can be shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize What People Need and Want to Know
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on information that audiences consider most important: immediate risks, protective actions, access to services, and what will change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize content around audience questions (Is it safe? What should I do? Where can I get help?). Omit or move technical background lower in the release. Use FAQs to address common concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor Messages and Channels to Audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt wording, examples, tone, and distribution channels for different demographic, cultural, and professional audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify priority audiences (e.g., parents, healthcare workers, seniors) and produce core messages plus audience-specific versions. Use translated materials, social media, press briefings, hotlines, and community partners as appropriate. Measure reach and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate and Align with Partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure messaging is coordinated across agencies, jurisdictions, and partner organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish agreed key messages and timelines with partners before public release. Use joint statements when appropriate. Avoid mixed or contradictory guidance that confuses the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Right Tone: Calm, Confident, Caring
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a tone that conveys competence and concern without causing panic or downplaying risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance urgency with reassurance; be neither alarmist nor dismissive. Match tone to the situation’s seriousness and audience needs. Spokespeople should speak plainly and empathetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide Sources, Resources, and Next Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Include authoritative sources, contact information, and links to where people can get more details or assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of the release, list websites, phone numbers, clinic locations, and times for updates. Make it easy to follow up. Anti-pattern: vague referrals like 'contact your provider' without contact details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update Frequently and Correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a predictable cadence of updates and correct earlier information openly when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule and announce next-update times; issue corrections promptly and explain reasons for changes. Consistent update practice reduces rumor and maintains engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Jargon and Technical Overload
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume technical literacy; translate technical terms into practical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If technical terms are necessary, define them briefly and relate them to everyday decisions. Anti-pattern: long technical explanations that obscure actionable advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and Address Misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proactively identify likely rumors or misunderstandings and address them clearly in releases or FAQs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor social media and partner feedback; include myth-versus-fact sections when needed. Correct false claims with facts and sources, without amplifying fringe conspiracies unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Accessible Materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure press releases and supplemental materials are accessible to people with disabilities and limited literacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide alt text for images, easy‑read summaries, translated versions, and formats compatible with screen readers. Use clear fonts and sufficient contrast for posted PDFs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Evidence and Explain Rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When recommending actions, explain briefly the evidence or logic so people understand the reason and are more likely to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite data, observable risks, or expert rationale in one or two sentences. Avoid long scientific digressions; keep rationale directly tied to recommended action.
